distribution.name: Figure 1 Geological map with volcanic ash layer.jpg
distribution.description: Fig. 1. Geographical and geological overview of the Ries impact structure (based on Ernstson, 1974; Pohl et al., 1977; Hüttner and Schmidt-Kaler, 1999) and location of the drilling sites Nördlinger Ries 1003 (NR1003) and Nördlingen 1973. Lithostratigraphic subdivision of the sedimentary crater fill based on Jankowski (1981). For exact occurrence of volcanic ash layer in the lake deposits, readers are referred to Arp et al. (2021).

distribution.name: Figure 2. Columnar section.jpg
distribution.description: Fig. 2. Sedimentary profile of the NR1003 drill core and profiles of carbonate contents in different phases (left), stable carbon and oxygen isotopes (right). Clay, marl (or dolomite marl) and limestone (or dolostone) are defined by <25% CaCO3, 25–75% CaCO3, >75% CaCO3 (or equivalent CaMg(CO3)2). Likewise, the microcrystalline calcite, calcite-rich mixture, dolomite-rich mixture and microcrystalline dolomite are defined by >75 mol% calcite, 50-75 mol % calcite, 50–75 mol % dolomite and >75 mol % dolomite. See Table S3 for detailed Ccarb and Table S4 and S5 for XRD data, Table S6 for stable isotope data. Note that the dolomite in the left column refers to the calculated dolomite content, on basis of Ccarb and relative intensity of dolomite peak (hkl 104) in XRD patterns (Table S4). Only dolomite (i.e. no subdivision between ferroan and Ca-rich dolomite) is shown here (see 3.3). The age of the volcanic ash layer is derived from Arp et al. (2021).

distribution.name: Figure 3 Lithofacies figure.jpg
distribution.description: Fig. 3. Petrographic features of Ries lacustrine deposits. A: Laminated marlstone with fluid escape structures in the basal member. Note the trails of upwelling flows as indicated by arrows, formed tepee-like deformations (white arrows) and chamber-like matrixes (black arrows) that were capped during fluid upwelling. Open millimetre-scale pores or voids in the lower part, white-grey laminated marlstone might suggest escaped gas inclusions in the past. B: Matrix-supported breccia in the diatom smbr (98.5 to 99.3 m depth), at left side is a reworked laminite clast; at the right side is a reworked unstratified marl/dolomitic marl intraclast. C and D: mud cracks at 76.47 and 80.49 m depth (varicolored-marl smbr). E: tubular traces of bioturbation in unstratified marlstones at 42.65 m depth (dolomite-marl smbr). F: laminated dolomite and bituminous shale with remnants of fish in the analcime smbr (217.6 to 218.6 m depth). G: cut slab of a typical sample with high δ13C values (NR1003-156, 116.7 m depth, diatom smbr): white-grey stratified argillaceous marlstone (upper part) and greenish medium-grey laminated marlstone with bituminous intercalations (lower part). H: marlstone sample from the high δ13C interval but with normal δ13C values (NR1003-157, 118.7 m depth, diatom smbr).

distribution.name: Figure 4 Columnar section geochemistry.jpg
distribution.description: Fig. 4. Element ratios (Si/Al, K/Al, Zr/Al and Ba/Al) from bulk μ-XRF elemental analyses (Table S8) of the carbonate-bearing marlstone samples.

distribution.name: Figure 5 Biomarker_Columnar section-R2.jpg
distribution.description: Fig. 5. Columnar section showing total organic carbon (TOC), δ13C (carbonate), pristane/phytane ratios (Pr/Ph), and abundances of selected biomarkers in μg/g TOC (carbonate-free fraction). For detailed results and abbreviations please see also Table 2 and 4.2.2, and Fig. S5 for chemical structures.

distribution.name: Figure 6 Isotope covariation_Ries_New_Figure_v2.jpg
distribution.description: Fig. 6. Stable carbon–oxygen covariation plots of the samples from the laminated marlstone section (226 to 87.3 m core depth). A: samples from the high δ13C interval (upper laminite member and varicolored smbr, symbols with black outlines), analcime smbr (red-outlined symbols) and clinoptilolite smbr (purple-outlined symbols); note that most of the samples are dolomites. The covariation trend line is calculated based on calcite and calcite-rich mixture samples from clinoptilolite to varicolored-marl smbr. B: Calcite and calcite-rich samples from NR1003 (black symbols) and Nördlingen 1973 (grey-filled symbols, Rothe and Hoefs, 1977); Miocene (pre-impact) floodplain carbonate (blue-outlined and yellow-filled symbols) at Pleinfeld locality, ca. 30 km away from the Ries crater (Zeng et al., 2021) and with their mean δ18O values representing the meteoric calcite line.

distribution.name: Figure 7 high-d13C-dolomite-Ries-1.jpg
distribution.description: Fig. 7. Interpretations of pore water biogeochemical processes, lake physiochemistry and solute provenance of the Ries crater lake based on observations from this study. TSR: thermochemical sulfate reduction; MSR: microbial sulfate reduction; MOX: aerobic methane oxidation. The gypsum pseudomorphs in the clay member were reported by Arp et al. (2017) and in basal member by Jankowski (1981); thiophenes in clinoptilolite smbr was reported by Barakat and Rullk¨otter (1997) otherwise in this study; occurrences of diatoms by (Schauderna, 1983). The estimated lake level curve is based on sedimentological observations (e.g. lamination, bioturbation, slumping, mud cracks, in-situ brecciation) in this study and diatom associations in drill core N¨ordlingen 1973 (Schauderna, 1983). The estimated salinity was depicted schematically from indicative organic compounds (Zhao et al., 2022a). The δ15N values schematically correlate with lake water pH variations, with support from hydrochemical modeling results (Stüeken et al., 2020). S isotope data of sedimentary sulfides from drill core N¨ordlingen 1973 were adopted and modified from Tino et al. (2023).

distribution.name: FIgure 8-Model single column-Siltingup effect-low H2S analcime.jpg
distribution.description: Fig. 8. Models of carbonate formation coupled with hydrochemistry and biogeochemistry. A1, B1, C1 and D1: scenarios of carbonate-poor beds due to lower salinity; A2, B2, C2, D2: scenarios of intensive carbonate formation (carbonate-rich beds) due to high salinity. A). The early Ries crater lake (clinoptilolite smbr) with a high sulfate level due to sulfate-rich groundwaters discharged from the crystalline basement. More Ca-rich dolomite is present in A2 than in the carbonate-poor bed (A1). The subsequent phase is characterized by a large lake volume and decreased salinity (analcime smbr, B). Note that 1) no major methanogenesis is evident in A and B; 2) considerable dissolved iron was present in B; 3) a presumed lower sulfate concentration in B as indicated by width of the sulfate curve than A. B1: marcasite and siderite formed at the time of the carbonate-poor interval; B2: ankerite and Ca-rich dolomite formed during the interval of intensive carbonate formation, as a result of high iron availability in porewaters. C) As ongoing iron and sulfate reduction further led to a low-sulfate interval, methanogenesis started and resulted in an enriched 13C DIC (high δ13C interval). Episodical inflow derived from Bunte Breccia and recurring stratification caused fluctuating physio-chemical conditions, facilitating Ostwald’s ripening process to promote dolomite formation in high 13C DIC environments. C1: in the carbonate-poor interval, biogenic primary calcites and Ca-rich dolomite formed, and small framboidal pyrites (<5μm) formed in the water column; C2: at the time of intensive carbonate formation, Ca-rich dolomite formed following an increase in salinity. D) Following the lake level drop, dissolved oxygen reached the lake bottom and caused a downward shift of the anaerobic zone (dolomite-marl smbr and upper clay member). MOX: aerobic methanotrophy. D1: framboidal pyrites (>5μm) formed in sediments during a carbonate-poor interval; D2: Ca-rich dolomite and calcite precipitated at a time of intensive carbonate formation.

distribution.name: R1-Fig S1 lithofacies +fossils.jpg
distribution.description: Figure S1 Different lithofacies and fossils from drill core NR 1003. A: Conglomerate and coarse-grained pebbly sandstone in the basal member (242.0 to 242.8 m depth), containing pebbles reworked from crystalline basement rocks of the inner ring. B: Well-preserved fish from the laminite member (diatom subunit, 106 m depth). C: Artemia faecal pellets from laminite member (clinoptilolite subunit, 216.6 m depth). D: Dark grey to black stratified lignite with elemental sulphur from present-day sulfide oxidation. E: Pedoturbation/pedogenic slickenside in the dark grey and ochre-brown mottling carbonaceous claystone (clay member, 22.0 to 22.2 m depth). F. Hydrobia trochulus and shell debris from the clay member (38.4 m depth). G. Gyraulus and shell debris from clay member (30.26 m depth). H: Compressed shell debris of Planorbarius (clay member, 32.0 m depth). I: Desiccation crack with in-situ brecciation (clay member, 32.1 m depth).

distribution.name: R1-Fig S10 -High d13C interval C-O-Ccarb.jpg
distribution.description: Figure S10. Correlation plots between δ13C, δ18O values and bulk carbonate contents (C carb) in dolomite and dolomite-rich samples from the high δ13C interval. The moderate to strong covariations between δ13C and δ18O values can be explained by coupled short-term hydrological and biogeochemical variations. When the freshwater influx was lower, the water body became more stagnant and saline (consequently higher δ18O values), thus facilitating anaerobic respiration and scavenging inhibitors for methanogenesis (e.g., sulfate). These processes led to the high δ13C values in the dolomite-rich samples. At times of higher freshwater influxes, dolomite formation ceases due to a lower cation concentration in the porewater, whereas a greater amount of low-δ18O calcites form from water column. The δ13C values of these calcites mainly reflect evaporation and photosynthesis effects from lake surface. While minor dolomites still form in the stratified lake bottom with higher 13C DIC, intermediate bulk δ18O-δ13C values are found in dolomite-calcite mixtures (Table S6). Shallow burial or late diagenetic events do not explain the observations.

distribution.name: R1-Fig S2 Basal member lithology.jpg
distribution.description: Figure S2. Core image of carbonate-bearing section in the basal member. The laminated marlstone with fluid escape structures between 242.41 to 243.7 m is typical for upper part of sedimentary cycle in the basal member. Between 238.4 to 242.41 m comprises the lower-middle part of the cycle, which contain pebbly sandstone/fine-grained conglomerate to fine-grained calcareous sandstone or calcareous siltstone.

distribution.name: R1-Fig S3 EMPA photomicrographs.jpg
distribution.description: Figure S3. Photomicrographs of carbonates in the Miocene Ries crater lake. A: close-up of a laminated marlstone from the basal member, with light-colored calcite laminae and dark-colored dolomite-rich laminae. Note the higher smectite/siliciclastic contents in the dolomite-rich laminae. B: close-up of calcites and dolomite from the basal member. Note some core or zonation is shown in the dark colored subeuhedral dolomite. C: close-up of Ca-rich dolomites from the clinoptilolite smbr. Note that most dolomites are surrounded by smectites and some submicrometer euhedral dolomites formed in interstitial spaces (white square). D: Ca-rich dolomite (Ca-dol), ankerite (ank) and iron sulfide/monosulfide (is) at the analcime smbr. Note that some Ca-rich dolomite and ankerite formed at the rim of iron sulfide. E: round or subround pellets (40 – 60 µm wide), filled with Ca-rich dolomites. F: mosaiced Ca-rich dolomite, ankerite (white rectangle) and submicrometer euhedral Ca-rich dolomite ininterstitial spaces. G: concretion of chalcedony (q: quartz) at the analcime smbr, whose outer rim is partly replaced by twinning-spearheaded marcasite (m, e.g. Schieber, 2011). H: 30-µm-sized siderite (sid) aggregate.

distribution.name: R1-Fig S4 EMPA 2.jpg
distribution.description: Figure S4. Photomicrographs of carbonates from the Miocene Ries crater lake. A: close-up of a marlstone sample (bulk δ13C = +5.51‰, δ18O = +0.70‰) in the high δ13C interval, containing medium-grey Ca-rich dolomite and white-grey siderite. Siderites (white squares) are euhedral to subeuhedral, often with etched surfaces and twinning edges (white arrows). B: close-up of the marlstone sample that shows framboidal pyrites (bulk δ13C = +6.97‰, δ18O = +0.33‰), which were detected for the first time from downcore to top (NR1003-164, 131.6 m core depth). Note the submicrometer Ca-rich dolomite (black arrows) and white-grey thin, linear structure resembling extracelluar polymeric substance (EPS, white arrow). C: zoom-out of the marlstone sample (NR1003-8, bulk δ13C = +17.03‰, δ18O = +2.12‰, 121.6 m core depth), showing dolomite-poor, bioclast-rich lamina between the white dashed line and dolomite-rich laminae outside the dashed line. Note that the bioclast is encrusted by Ca-rich dolomites (EPS?). For dolomite-rich laminae, Ca-rich dolomites form thicker sheaths (white arrows) than the bioclast-rich lamina (black arrows). D: close-up of Ca-rich dolomite sheaths (white arrows) and disordered Ca-rich dolomite cores (black arrows) inside the biogenic tube structures (147.8 m core depth, bulk δ13C = +12.94‰, δ18O = +3.88‰). E: rhombohedral stoichiometric dolomite (98.1 m core depth, bulk δ13C = +16.40‰, δ18O = +0.28‰). F: white-grey submicrometer-sized Ca-rich dolomite and calcified green algae (white arrows) at 74.4 core depth (bulk δ13C = +6.99‰, δ18O = +1.38‰). F: subeuhedral to euhedral Ca-rich dolomites, filling the pore spaces between smectites. White arrows refer framboidal pyrites (38.9 core depth, bulk δ13C = +2.46‰, δ18O = +0.32‰). G: rhombohedral Ca-rich dolomites and framboidal pyrites (white square, 33.3 m core depth, bulk δ13C = +0.94‰, δ18O = -0.30‰).
